summary: Lists functional requirements that fed into the design of LDP extensions for point-to-multipoint label switched paths in MPLS. The work was overtaken by a different protocol solution from the MPLS working group, so this document is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Before building something, you write down what it must do. This is that list for sending one stream to many places in MPLS networks, but a different design won out. It is historic.

subtitle: Functional requirements for extending LDP to support one-to-many routing.

tldr.problem: Network operators need to deliver point-to-multipoint traffic (one sender to many receivers) efficiently over MPLS, but the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) was originally designed only for point-to-point (one-to-one) connections.
tldr.mechanism: This document lists detailed requirements for extending LDP to set up and manage point-to-multipoint label switched paths (LSPs), where traffic is replicated at branch routers instead of being duplicated at the source.
tldr.outcome: A solution was developed but did not closely follow these requirements; the document is published as a historic record of the ideas that shaped the protocol work.

today: RFC 6348 is Historic. The MPLS working group developed Multipoint LDP (mLDP), which provides point-to-multipoint and multipoint-to-multipoint LSPs. While mLDP addresses the core need, the published specification did not closely follow the requirements in RFC 6348. Nonetheless, P2MP delivery remains important for IPTV, multicast VPNs, and other services, and mLDP is deployed in production networks. The requirements in this document remain a useful reference for understanding what P2MP routing needs to accomplish.

sections.title: The Need for Point-to-Multipoint
sections.content:
Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) uses labels to forward packets along predetermined paths called Label Switched Paths (LSPs). Originally, LDP only supported point-to-point LSPs (one sender, one receiver) and multipoint-to-point LSPs (many senders, one receiver). As service providers began offering multicast services—including Voice over IP with multiple listeners and IPTV—they needed point-to-multipoint LSPs: one sender reaching many receivers.

Naively, a provider could create separate point-to-point LSPs from the sender to each receiver, but this wastes bandwidth: the same packet travels the same link multiple times, once for each receiver. Instead, point-to-multipoint allows traffic to be replicated only at branch points in the tree, so each link carries at most one copy of each packet.
sections.plainLanguage: If one person wants to send the same message to ten people, you could send ten separate letters. Or you could send one letter to a distribution hub and let them make copies and forward them. Point-to-multipoint routing does the second thing, saving bandwidth.

sections.title: How Point-to-Multipoint Works
sections.content:
A point-to-multipoint LSP consists of a single Ingress LSR (the sender) and one or more Egress LSRs (receivers). Traffic flows from the ingress through a tree of routers. Routers along the path are called Transit LSRs; those that forward traffic to multiple downstream routers are Branch LSRs, and they perform the critical function of replicating traffic. Receivers can be added to or removed from a P2MP LSP dynamically: a new receiver can "join" the tree, and an intermediate router becomes a branch point to reach it.

The document also considers multipoint-to-multipoint (MP2MP) LSPs, where any of a group of routers can be both senders and receivers. This is useful for applications like video conferencing. An MP2MP LSP is typically built from two trees: an upstream tree carrying traffic to a root, and a downstream tree carrying traffic from the root.
sections.plainLanguage: A point-to-multipoint tree has one starting point (the sender) and multiple end points (the receivers). Traffic is copied only where the tree branches. Routers can join or leave the tree as needed.

sections.title: Key Requirements
sections.content:
The requirements document specifies several crucial capabilities. The mechanism must scale to tens of thousands of P2MP trees with hundreds or thousands of leaves each, and the state stored at each router should depend only on how many neighbors it has on the tree, not the total tree size. Adding or removing a leaf must not disrupt data transfer to other leaves: no packet loss, duplication, or unexpected delays.

Loop detection and avoidance are critical, especially for MP2MP where routers may receive traffic on multiple interfaces. Nodes must detect routing loops but do so without impacting scalability. The mechanism must support rerouting upon network failures, better paths becoming available, or planned maintenance. P2MP LSPs must work correctly when nested inside P2P or P2MP traffic engineering tunnels, and the system must handle both IPv4 and IPv6, work across multiple IGP areas and Autonomous Systems, and maintain backward compatibility with existing point-to-point LDP operations.

Operations, Administration and Maintenance (OAM) tools must allow operators to check connectivity, trace the path of a P2MP LSP, and detect data plane failures quickly. The solution should support graceful restart and fault recovery mechanisms so that temporary network disruptions do not destroy LSP state unnecessarily.
sections.plainLanguage: The system must handle thousands of trees, let leaves join and leave without disrupting others, detect loops, automatically reroute around failures, work with both old and new routing systems, and give operators tools to debug problems.

sections.title: Design Challenges
sections.content:
The document notes several inherent tensions in the design. Scalability vs. information: to avoid routing loops, nodes may need to know which other routers are on the tree, but this information can become unwieldy as trees grow. Leaf-initiated setup vs. ingress control: Should leaves discover the ingress and join independently, or should the ingress control which receivers are added? Leaf-initiated setup scales better with many leaves but requires leaves to know the P2MP tree identifier somehow.

Data duplication during rerouting is difficult to avoid: if the tree is being reconfigured around a failure, receivers might temporarily get multiple copies of packets until the old path is fully torn down. Multi-access networks (like Ethernet LANs) add complexity: if multiple potential upstream routers exist on the same LAN, all downstream routers must choose the same upstream peer, or replication wastes bandwidth. The solution must also coexist peacefully with P2P LSPs, RSVP-TE based P2MP TE tunnels, and potentially P2MP LSPs from other mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: Building point-to-multipoint routing is hard because you want to scale to many trees and many leaves, but knowing enough about the tree to avoid loops and handle failures requires trading off complexity and information.

sections.title: Shared Trees and MP2MP
sections.content:
For a group of routers that all need to send and receive to each other (like a group of video conference endpoints), a shared tree is more efficient than individual P2MP trees from each sender. A shared tree typically uses a root LSR as an anchor point: all members send traffic upstream to the root, and the root sends traffic downstream to all members. This reduces the amount of control and forwarding state each router must maintain, especially compared to having N separate P2MP LSPs for N members.

The document recommends defining multiple root LSRs (a primary and backup) for redundancy. It also notes an important constraint: receivers must not receive back packets they themselves sent on the MP2MP LSP (otherwise a video conference would see feedback). The solution should minimize delays between any pair of leaves and allow operators to check bidirectional connectivity.
sections.plainLanguage: If many routers need to talk to each other, instead of drawing a P2MP tree from each one to all others, you can use a shared tree with one root router to reduce complexity.
